title: Genghis Khan
subtitle: The outcast who built the largest land empire in history

package.intro: Genghis Khan began life as an abandoned outcast on the Mongolian steppe and died ruling an empire from northern China to the Caspian Sea. His conquests killed on a scale few events in history can match; his empire also connected the world as never before. This documentary tells both stories.
facts: Born Temüjin around 1162 near the Onon River, in present-day Mongolia
Proclaimed Genghis Khan at a great assembly on the Onon in 1206
Invaded the Jin dynasty of northern China in 1211; its capital Zhongdu (Beijing) fell in 1215
A Mongol trade caravan was massacred at Otrar, in the Khwarazmian Empire, in 1218
Invaded the Khwarazmian Empire in 1219; Bukhara, Samarkand, Urgench, Merv and Nishapur fell by 1221
Died in August 1227 during a campaign against the Western Xia; his burial place is unknown
His successors created the largest contiguous land empire in history
A 2003 genetic study suggested about 0.5% of men worldwide carry a Y-chromosome lineage possibly descended from his family
package.sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, The Secret History of the Mongols, Ata-Malik Juvayni's History of the World Conqueror, Timothy May's The Mongol Conquests in World History, Jack Weatherford's Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World, Zerjal et al. (2003), American Journal of Human Genetics.

sections.name: Cold open

lines.title: GENGHIS KHAN
lines.sub: The outcast who built the largest land empire in history

lines: Early in 1221, a Mongol army surrounded Merv, one of the great cities of Central Asia. After it surrendered, its people were led out onto the plain, and most of them were killed.
A chronicler of the time claimed seven hundred thousand died there. Modern historians think that number is impossible. But Merv never regained its old greatness.

lines.label: estimated deaths in all the Mongol conquests · highly uncertain

lines: Estimates for all the Mongol conquests run into the tens of millions. Yet the man who began them is honoured today as the founder of a nation.
Genghis Khan is remembered as one of history's most destructive conquerors, and in Mongolia as its greatest hero. Both memories rest on real events.

sections.name: The outcast
lines: He was born around 1162, near the Onon River in what is now Mongolia, and named Temüjin. His father, Yesügei, was a minor chief.

The steppe was a world of feuding clans who herded horses and sheep and lived in felt tents. Most of what we know of his youth comes from one source, The Secret History of the Mongols, written after his death.
When Temüjin was about nine, his father was poisoned by enemies from the Tatar tribe. His clan abandoned the widow and her children, who survived by gathering roots and fishing.
As a teenager he killed his half-brother, Begter, in a quarrel over food. His mother condemned him furiously.
Later he was captured by a rival clan and held with a heavy wooden collar locked around his neck. He escaped at night, hidden by a sympathetic family.

sections.name: The rise

lines.name: Temüjin
lines.role: Abandoned chief's son who united the Mongol tribes.

lines: Temüjin grew into a shrewd and magnetic young leader, gathering followers one by one.

lines.name: Börte
lines.role: Temüjin's first wife. Mother of his four principal sons.

lines: He married Börte, the girl he had been promised to as a boy. When raiders from the Merkit tribe kidnapped her, he won her back with the help of two powerful allies.
One was Toghrul, khan of the Kereit people. The other was Jamukha, his childhood friend and sworn blood brother. Both would later become his enemies.
Over the next twenty years he fought his way to the top. He promoted men for loyalty and talent rather than noble birth, and shared plunder with his followers.
He crushed the Tatars, who had killed his father, and had most of their men put to death.
He defeated Toghrul, then the Naimans, and finally Jamukha, who was betrayed by his own followers and executed.
In 1206, a great assembly of the tribes proclaimed him Genghis Khan. The exact meaning of the title is debated. It may mean fierce ruler, or universal ruler.

sections.name: The war machine
lines: He reorganised his people into units of ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand, mixing up the old tribes so that loyalty ran to him. He adopted a writing system and a code of law.
Every soldier was a mounted archer, with several horses each. Mongol armies moved fast, scouted far ahead, and were masters of the feigned retreat.
He also began a system of relay stations, where messengers could change horses, carrying orders across vast distances at remarkable speed.

lines.text: Surrender and be spared. Resist and be destroyed.

lines: His method was simple and brutal. Cities that surrendered were usually spared, though heavily taxed. Cities that resisted were often destroyed, and their people killed or enslaved, as a warning to the next.

sections.name: China
lines: In 1209 he forced the Western Xia kingdom to submit. In 1211 he invaded the Jin dynasty, which ruled northern China.
In 1215 the Jin capital, Zhongdu, today's Beijing, fell after a long siege, and was sacked and burned.
He was also a fast learner. Captured Chinese engineers taught the Mongols siege warfare, and skilled craftsmen were often spared and put to work.

sections.name: The western war
lines: To the west lay the Khwarazmian Empire, stretching across Central Asia and Iran. In 1218, a trade caravan sent by Genghis Khan was massacred at the border city of Otrar.
He sent envoys to demand justice. The Shah, Muhammad the Second, had one of them executed and sent the others back humiliated.
In 1219 Genghis Khan invaded with a huge army. Over the next three years, Bukhara, Samarkand, Urgench, Merv and Nishapur fell one after another.

lines.text: If you had not committed great sins, God would not have sent a punishment like me upon you.
lines.who: Genghis Khan at Bukhara, 1220, according to the historian Juvayni

lines: At Bukhara, according to the Persian historian Juvayni, he told the city's leading men that he was God's punishment for their sins.

Chroniclers recorded death tolls of hundreds of thousands, even more than a million, for single cities. Ibn al-Athir and Juvayni gave these figures for Merv. Modern historians consider them impossible, but agree the slaughter was immense.
Irrigation systems were wrecked and farmland turned to waste. Some historians argue parts of the region took centuries to recover.
The Shah fled west and died on an island in the Caspian Sea, his empire gone.
Two of Genghis Khan's generals rode on around the Caspian, through the Caucasus, and defeated an army of Rus' princes in 1223, before turning home.

sections.name: Death
lines: In 1226 he turned on the Western Xia, who had refused to send troops for his western war. He died during the campaign, in August 1227. The cause is unknown. One account says he never recovered from a fall from his horse.
The Western Xia kingdom was destroyed soon afterwards, and many of its people were killed.

lines.text: His grave has never been found.

lines: He was buried in secret, somewhere in Mongolia. His grave has never been found.

sections.name: The empire
lines: His sons and grandsons carried the conquests further: across Russia, into Hungary and Poland, to Baghdad in 1258, and over all of China by 1279. It became the largest contiguous land empire in history.
In northern China, census figures fell by tens of millions within a generation. Historians caution that part of the drop reflects flight, chaos and people who simply went uncounted.

lines.head: The Mongol peace
items: Safer trade on the Silk Road

lines: Once the conquests ended, the empire linked China, Persia and Europe. Merchants and envoys, like the Venetian Marco Polo decades later, crossed it in relative safety, and goods and ideas moved between continents.
The same routes may also have helped carry the Black Death west in the 1340s, though historians still debate exactly how.

sections.name: Legacy

lines.label: men worldwide carry a lineage a 2003 study linked to his family

lines: In 2003, a genetic study found that about one in two hundred men alive today carry a Y-chromosome lineage that the authors suggested came from Genghis Khan's family. Not all scientists agree.

lines.name: Genghis Khan
lines.role: Founder of the Mongol Empire. Mongolia's national hero.

lines: In Mongolia, his memory was played down under Soviet influence. Since the democratic revolution of 1990, he has returned as the father of the nation, on banknotes, on the capital's airport, and as a giant steel statue on the steppe.
To Mongolians, he made a scattered people into a nation and a world power. In Iran, Central Asia and China, he is remembered for the cities that vanished.
Both memories are true. His empire connected the world on a scale never seen before, and it was built on a scale of killing that is almost as hard to imagine.
